review_authority_note: Reviewer cited SLE-MASTER-001 v1.1.0; GitHub current main is v1.2.1. Current-standard compatibility remains a separate release gate.

entries.example: The classroom was quiet before the lesson.
entries.note: Past simple changes with the subject: I/he/she/it was; you/we/they were. Present forms are am/is/are.
entries.common_error: Avoid *I were late* in an ordinary past statement; special hypothetical were is a separate advanced pattern.

entries.example: Mina did her homework before dinner.
entries.note: Past simple did; past participle done normally follows an auxiliary such as have/has.
entries.common_error: Avoid *I have did*; distinguish main verb do from auxiliary do.

entries.example: We had a short meeting after school.
entries.note: Have is also an auxiliary in perfect forms; the three-form table describes the lexical verb.
entries.common_error: Avoid *I have have breakfast yesterday*; a finished yesterday action normally takes had.

entries.meaning: move towards a place or speaker
entries.example: My cousin came to our school festival.
entries.note: The base and past participle are the same; came is the past simple.
entries.common_error: Avoid *has came*; use has come.

entries.example: She took her umbrella on the trip.
entries.note: Taken is the past participle: have taken.
entries.common_error: Avoid *have took*; use have taken.

entries.example: The teacher gave us useful advice.
entries.note: Given is the past participle: has given.
entries.common_error: Avoid *have gave*; use have given.

entries.example: We made a poster for the science fair.
entries.note: Made is both the simple past and past participle.
entries.common_error: Remember make a decision and make progress; do not treat every noun combination as make.

entries.example: I knew the answer after reading the clue.
entries.note: Known is the participle; have known may describe a state continuing to now.
entries.common_error: Avoid *have knew*.

entries.example: We thought the timetable was clear.
entries.note: Thought is both the simple past and past participle.
entries.common_error: Avoid *thinked*; distinguish opinion think from planning/thinking about.

entries.meaning: help someone learn a skill or subject
entries.example: Our coach taught us a new warm-up routine.
entries.note: Taught is both the simple past and past participle.
entries.common_error: Avoid *teached*; note the spelling differs from catch—caught.

entries.example: I read the whole story yesterday.
entries.note: Written forms are identical, but base is pronounced /riːd/ and past/participle /red/.
entries.common_error: Past spelling alone cannot signal the tense; use context or audio.

entries.example: I put the worksheet in my folder yesterday.
entries.note: All three forms are spelled put.
entries.common_error: Avoid *putted* for the usual verb meaning place.

entries.example: They ate lunch in the school garden.
entries.note: Eaten is used after have/has in the perfect.
entries.common_error: Avoid *have ate*; use have eaten.

entries.example: She spoke to the librarian about the book.
entries.note: Spoken is the past participle; spoke is the simple past.
entries.common_error: Avoid *have spoke*; use have spoken.

entries.example: We found the missing pencil under the desk.
entries.note: Found is both simple past and past participle.
entries.common_error: Distinguish find—found—found from found—founded—founded meaning establish.

entries.example: The route was long, but the group enjoyed the walk.
entries.note: Joins contrasting clauses within one sentence; a comma is common before but when both sides are independent clauses.
entries.common_error: Not interchangeable with however without changing punctuation.

entries.example: I took a jacket because the room was cold.
entries.note: Because introduces a clause with a subject and verb; the order can be reversed.
entries.common_error: Do not write *because of it was cold*.

entries.example: The match stopped because of the heavy rain.
entries.note: It is followed by a noun phrase, pronoun or appropriate -ing phrase, not an ordinary finite clause.
entries.common_error: Contrast because + subject and verb.
entries.construction: main clause + because of + noun phrase / -ing phrase

entries.example: Although it was raining, we still played outside.
entries.note: Connects a concession to a main clause; a comma typically separates an initial subordinate clause.
entries.common_error: Do not double-link as *Although it rained, but we went out*.

entries.example: Despite the rain, the event continued.
entries.note: Despite normally takes a noun phrase or -ing phrase; despite the fact that + clause is a distinct expanded structure.
entries.common_error: Do not write *despite it was raining*.
entries.construction: Despite + noun phrase / -ing phrase, + main clause

entries.example: The test was difficult. However, everyone finished on time.
entries.note: Connects independent sentences or suitably punctuated clauses; at sentence start it is often followed by a comma.
entries.common_error: Avoid the comma splice *The test was difficult, however we finished*.

entries.example: The library was closed. Therefore, we studied at home.
entries.note: Signals that the next statement is a conclusion or result supported by the first.
entries.common_error: Not a simple drop-in replacement for so with the same punctuation; do not infer certainty without evidence.

entries.example: There are many free ways to practise English. For example, you can read short stories.
entries.note: Introduce an actual example that supports the preceding point.
entries.common_error: One example does not prove every case; avoid repeating it without added detail.
entries.construction: general claim. For example, + specific illustration

entries.example: The club offers reading groups. In addition, it runs a weekly writing workshop.
entries.note: Adds a genuinely new supporting point; commonly followed by a comma at the start of a sentence.
entries.common_error: Do not use it merely to make a short paragraph sound formal.
entries.construction: Sentence A. In addition, sentence B.

entries.example: First, read the question and underline the key task.
entries.note: Marks the opening step of a real procedure, plan or ordered explanation.
entries.common_error: Not every paragraph or essay needs numbered First/Second/Finally signposts.

entries.example: Finally, check your paragraph for missing details.
entries.note: Marks the last step of an ordered sequence; can also mean after a long wait in other contexts.
entries.common_error: Do not confuse last step with an unsupported conclusion.

entries.example: In conclusion, the class should keep the library open after school because more students could use it.
entries.note: Reserve for a real summary or synthesis in an extended text; not a mandatory sentence opener.
entries.common_error: Avoid adding it to a two-sentence answer or repeating the introduction without insight.

entries.meaning: Normally suggests every relevant occasion; actual habitual claims can depend on context.
entries.example: I always check my bag before school.
entries.note: Normally suggests every relevant occasion; actual habitual claims can depend on context.
entries.common_error: Avoid treating this as a measured 100% statistic without counted evidence.
entries.position_rule: subject + always + main verb; be + always

entries.meaning: Describes a usual pattern with possible exceptions; frequency depends on the speaker's context.
entries.example: We usually eat dinner together.
entries.note: Describes a usual pattern with possible exceptions; frequency depends on the speaker's context.
entries.common_error: Do not assign a universal numerical percentage.
entries.position_rule: subject + usually + main verb; be + usually

entries.meaning: Relatively frequent, but not an exact count; can appear in other positions for emphasis.
entries.example: My brother often rides his bike after school.
entries.note: Relatively frequent, but not an exact count; can appear in other positions for emphasis.
entries.common_error: Overlap with frequently and sometimes depends on circumstances.
entries.position_rule: subject + often + main verb; be + often

entries.meaning: Some occasions but not all; also commonly occurs at the beginning or end of a clause.
entries.example: I sometimes practise English before breakfast.
entries.note: Some occasions but not all; also commonly occurs at the beginning or end of a clause.
entries.common_error: Not exactly half of the time.
entries.position_rule: subject + sometimes + main verb; Sometimes, + clause

entries.meaning: Happens from time to time; sometimes and occasionally overlap in use.
entries.example: We occasionally visit the science museum.
entries.note: Happens from time to time; sometimes and occasionally overlap in use.
entries.common_error: Do not force a strict ranking against sometimes for every context.

entries.meaning: Means not often; may overlap with hardly ever depending on context.
entries.example: The school bus rarely arrives late.
entries.note: Means not often; may overlap with hardly ever depending on context.
entries.common_error: Avoid *do not rarely* for the intended meaning almost never in standard usage.
entries.position_rule: subject + rarely + main verb; be + rarely

entries.meaning: Means almost never; it already has negative meaning and does not need another not.
entries.example: I hardly ever watch television on weekdays.
entries.note: Means almost never; it already has negative meaning and does not need another not.
entries.common_error: Avoid *I don't hardly ever watch* in standard classroom writing.

entries.meaning: Expresses no occasions in the stated context; works with ordinary affirmative verb form.
entries.example: She never leaves her bicycle unlocked.
entries.note: Expresses no occasions in the stated context; works with ordinary affirmative verb form.
entries.common_error: Avoid *I don't never go* in standard English.
entries.position_rule: subject + never + main verb; be + never

entries.meaning: Names an approximate recurring schedule of one time per week, unlike usually.
entries.example: The drama club meets once a week.
entries.note: Names an approximate recurring schedule of one time per week, unlike usually.
entries.common_error: Does not tell you what percentage of days the action happens.

entries.meaning: Names two occurrences per month; calendars and month lengths vary.
entries.example: We visit the art gallery twice a month.
entries.note: Names two occurrences per month; calendars and month lengths vary.
entries.common_error: Do not automatically equate with every two weeks.

entries.meaning: Normally means on alternating days, roughly once every two days.
entries.example: I water the plants every other day.
entries.note: Normally means on alternating days, roughly once every two days.
entries.common_error: Not the same as every day or twice a week.
